Binance hack: Users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto heist - BBC News
Image source,ReutersByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporter
Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to bethe largest hack in history.
The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.
Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), haveaccused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack.
The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.
Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."
There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.
Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.
The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack.
Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.
Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back.
"We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme.
"The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added.
AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened
The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, whichstole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them.
The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets.
Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.
The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue.
Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected
Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said.
Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices.
Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally.

Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion breach
Anthony Ha8:20 AM PST · November 1, 2026
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance announced early on Sunday that it would begin allowing withdrawals in a phased process.
The company froze all deposits and withdrawals afterhackers stole $6.3 billion worth of cryptofrom Binance wallets. Inits latest update, Binance said it has now covered 95% of the stolen assets, and it’s still working to buy the “remaining affected assets,” which are “less liquid in the market and take longer time to source at the required scale.”
“Our commitment remains unchanged: Binance will bear the financial impact of the stolen funds,” the company added. “These losses will not be passed on to users.”
As for the withdrawal freeze, Binance said it did not make the decision lightly, as it understands “how important reliable access to withdrawals is for our users.” Nonetheless, the company said this was a necessary “precaution while our teams worked to contain the incident loss, assess its impact, restore affected services, and complete security checks.”
Binance will resume supporting withdrawals in phases, depending on network and asset type. As of Sunday morning, the company’snetwork status pageshowed a mix of normal, partially suspended, and fully suspended statuses — for example, Bitcoin withdrawals and deposits are still listed as partially suspended, while Ethereum deposits are normal and withdrawals are partially suspended.
The company also said users should expect “temporary delays or longer processing times due to traffic volume.”
“Resuming withdrawals is a major milestone, but our work continues,” Binance said. “We will continue strengthening our safeguards, completing the recovery process, and providing updates as progress continues.”
Binance subsequentlysharedthat between 6am and 3:30pm Coordinated Universal Time, it processed $4.6 billion in withdrawals and $1.0 billion in deposits, for a net outflow of $3.6 billion — 2.1% of its total assets under management.
The company also said it will publish a more in-depth incident report when its investigation is complete.
Binance previouslyblamed North Korea hackersfor the breach. On Saturday,the FBI saidthat a North Korean group known as TraderTraitor was responsible, and that the group was converting the assets primarily into Ethereum, with further laundering likely.

evidence_pages.https://www.wired.com/story/the-trump-ad:
The Trump Administration Is Wreaking Havoc on the Electoral System Before the Midterms | WIREDSkip to main content
Polls are looking prettybleak for Republicans—and the Trump administration’s various attempts tointerferewith the electionshaven’t been too successfuleither.
In recent weeks, the Department of Justice, helmed by Attorney General Todd Blanche, aproponent of conspiracy theoriesabout widespread noncitizen voting in the 2020 election, has pulled out all the stops to sow doubt in voters’ minds about the security and validity of the electoral process.
To do this, the DOJ has spent the last yeardemanding unredacted voter rolls,issuing executive ordersto wrest control of elections from states,raiding election offices, proposing new laws todisenfranchise millions of citizens, and claiming thatnoncitizenswere voting en masse across the country. (Incidents of verified noncitizen voting are vanishingly rare, as multiplebipartisaninvestigationshave shown.)
There have also been escalating threats by the DOJ against election officials. On Thursday,the DOJ sent lettersto election officials in all 50 states warning them that they would pursue criminal action if they failed to preserve election records for 22 days. Earlier that week, a federal judge had admonished the Trump administration for making similar threats around criminal prosecution against election officials in a different case.
“They're trying to create chaos and distrust in the system,” says Shelby Wayment, staff attorney at UCLA Law’s Safeguarding Democracy Project. “They're trying to file these now knowing they have virtually no chance of winning and then after they can claim the election was fraudulent.”
“This Department is following the facts and the law, not anyone’s political timetable,” a spokesperson for the DOJ tells WIRED, pointing out that the previous administration’s Justice departmentsued AlabamaandVirginiaahead of the 2024 election, claiming the DOJ was at the time trying “to stop them from removing suspected noncitizens from their voter rolls.”
Experts say that while the DOJ’s current legal efforts, including escalating fights inAlaskaandCaliforniaover candidates and voter rolls, are faltering, they’re also designed to lay the groundwork to question the results of this week’s vote.
“We have to expect absolutely, if the election doesn't go the way the president wants, that we will see the administration’s attempt to sow doubts in the election and maybe even challenge those results, but I'm also not worried about it,” David Becker, a former DOJ lawyer and the head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, tells WIRED.
“They have failed at everything they've tried to do. Our systems have held firm. Our institutions have held firm.”
34 federal district courts have ruled against Trump since he took office in 2025 blocking access to voter rolls and preventing executive orders being implemented, according toanalysis from the Brennan Center.
Former deputy assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division Justin Levitt thinks that a lot of the actions taken by the Trump administration are about a show of force and optics more than anything else. “What you’re seeing now is a ton of marketing. They are trying to communicate that they're in charge, and I think it's not working,” says Levitt, now a law professor at Loyola Marymount University. “But it is really important to remember that the federal government isn't in charge of the election process. State and local officials are.”
WIRED has laid out the details of the DOJ’s legal efforts in California, Nevada, Washington, and Alaska below, which have all been met with disdain from local and state officials.
California is officially a hotbed of election controversy. In October, theDOJ filed a federal lawsuitseeking a court order against California to compel them to sequester mail-in ballots associated with approximately 20,000 voters, claiming that these voters were noncitizens. On Wednesday, a federal judgein a strong-worded orderrejected the request.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” US District Judge David Carter wrote in his order filed late on Wednesday.
Almost immediately, the DOJ filed an appeal and a federal court quickly denied it.
The judge pointed out that similar claims from the administration about noncitizens on voter rolls hadn’t held up to scrutiny, and he had “further questions of credibility” about how they arrived at that number in the first place.
Last week, a federal judge also ruled that the DOJ had to turn over its list of around 20,000 names to the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, so that the group could analyze the dataset. On Saturday, the group submitted a legal filing stating that an analysis of the list found thatover 40 percent of the namesweren’t even in the state’s current voter files. In response, the DOJhas suggestedthat the publication of their analysis violated the terms of the lists released to them, and is urging a federal judge to consider whether contempt charges might be applicable here.
“The DOJ has clearly written rules that prevent it from engaging in any investigative activity close to an election—rules that private attorney Todd Blanche cited when representing his client, Donald Trump, in September 2024,” Becker says. “But the DOJ continues to violate its own policies.”
To cap it all off, the DOJissued grand jury subpoenasto California’s local election officials last week, indicating that despite repeated court losses it has no intention of backing down.
In October, the Justice Departmentfiled a lawsuitdesigned to block certification of the election result in Alaska’s Senate race if Democrat candidate Mary Peltola wins.
The reason for the lawsuit is the presence of a spoiler candidate on the ballot with a similar name as the incumbent Republican candidate Daniel Sullivan. The DOJ’s lawsuit was filed despite the Alaska Supreme Courtruling in the summerthat Daniel J. Sullivan Jr could remain on the ballot as no laws had been broken.

Nations Championship 2026: How are Ireland set for November Tests? - BBC Sport
Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,
Andy Farrell's side face Argentina and Fiji before renewing hostilities with South Africa this month
ByMatt GaultBBC Sport NI senior journalist
The last time Ireland entered an autumn schedule a year out from the Rugby World Cup, Andy Farrell's side were riding the crest of a wave.
Buoyed by their seismic Test series triumph over the All Blacks in New Zealand, Ireland dispatched South Africa, Fiji and Australia to end 2022 top of the world rankings.
At that point, their World Cup preparations were progressing smoothly.
But in the three years since the All Blacks exacted revenge in one of the great World Cup knockout matches in Paris, Ireland's place among rugby's elite has often looked less than assured.
Persistent defeats by New Zealand, South Africa and France have raised questions about the team's trajectory as next year's World Cup draws closer.
But with Argentina, Fiji and South Africa visiting Dublin over the next three weeks, Ireland have the opportunity to give their journey to Australia a much-needed shot in the arm.
Will the Ulsterman with farmer's strength be Ireland's next star?
Ireland 'optimistic' on Prendergast fitness
South Africa were 24-13 winners on their last visit to Dublin
The aforementioned sequence of poor results against rugby's heavyweights is a key concern.
Ireland have lost their past six meetings with New Zealand, France and South Africa by double-digit margins.
In those six games, they have scored 101 points and conceded 191, while the two most recent reverses - a 36-14 loss away to France in this year's Six Nations and July's 40-21 defeat inside the All Blacks' Eden Park fortress - were the heaviest.
It has not been all gloom, of course. The manner in which Ireland tore through England at Twickenham earlier this year was a thrilling reminder of their big-game prowess.
However, Farrell will be desperate for his side extinguish an error-prone performance in Auckland that allowed New Zealand to effectively wrap up the game by half-time.
To sufficiently alter the narrative, they must avoid first home losses to Argentina and Fiji before renewing hostilities with South Africa.
Last year, the Springboks devoured the Irish scrum in a 24-13 win in Dublin. Landing a knockout blow on the world champions at this stage in the cycle would be a significant statement.
In their quest for revenge, Ireland have placed an even greater emphasis on conditioning, with assistant coach Johnny Sexton saying they want it to be their "point of difference".
Whether that approach bears early fruit this month remains to be seen.
Tadhg Furlong's availability is a boost for Ireland
To topple the fearsome South African scrum, Farrell needs his strongest front row, so confirmation of Tadhg Furlong's availability will have been welcomed by the coaching team.
The three-time British and Irish Lions tourist was cleared by a disciplinary committee of grabbing Gavin Coombes in the groin during Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster.
With Furlong and fellow Lion Andrew Porter available, Farrell and scrum coach John Fogarty must devise a masterplan to establish Ireland a dominant set-piece force this month.
But Farrell has issues further back in the pack. With captain Caelan Doris and Jack Conan ruled out, Sean Jansen appears the frontrunner for the number eight jersey, although Dan Sheehan's run-out in the back row against Munster has raised the possibility of a more radical shake-up.
Uncapped Ulsterman James McNabney can fulfil that role, too, although the 23-year-old'srecent commentssuggest his playing time this month may be limited.
Ryan Baird's return offers another tried-and-tested option at blind-side flanker, with Tadhg Beirne and Cian Prendergast having featured there in the summer.
There is also uncertainty surrounding fly-half Sam Prendergast's fitness, with Jack Crowley already ruled out.
Prendergast has been nursing a wrist problem, and while Ireland said they were "optimistic" he will be available for selection, Ciaran Frawley may be afforded another opportunity at 10 following his impressive start to life at Connacht.
Ulster's Jamie Benson, a former England Under-20 international, is a more unknown quantity in the key playmaker role.
And with the injured Garry Ringrose unlikely to feature in November, Jamie Osborne - who played wing and full-back against Australia and Japan in the summer - could deputise at outside centre if Farrell decides against going for the more experienced Robbie Henshaw.
As for the wings, Mack Hansen's return is a welcome sight for Irish fans.
The 28-year-old, who missed the Six Nations and summer Tests, is a dynamic option out wide or at full-back, having scored a hat-trick of tries in the 15 jersey against Australia last year.
Argentina, Fiji and South Africa provide Ireland's opposition
Argentina have never beaten Ireland in Dublin but stunned the British and Irish Lions on their most recent visit to the Aviva Stadium last year.
Pumas head coach Felipe Contepomi has made three changes to his original 33-player squad as Facundo Isa, Rodrigo Martinez and Mateo Soler are late call-ups.
Captain Julian Montoya is one of a number of experienced players to return after missing out on the home defeats by South Africa and Australia in August, plus September's draw away to the Wallabies, but they will be without the injured Santiago Grondona, Ignacio Ruiz and Joaquin Oviedo.
Argentina are also without prop Thomas Gallo and utility back Santi Carreras, who impressed in the win over the Lions.
Those recent Tests saw Contepomi preside over a depleted squad, while in the summer, they suffered home defeats by England and Scotland, but did account for Wales.
Argentina play enterprising, free-flowing rugby but their form has been mixed, making them an intriguing opening opponent.
Fiji were beaten by Scotland, England and Wales during the southern hemisphere leg, but a Test win over Japan in October marked the first game in charge for new head coach Jake White, who led South Africa to World Cup glory in 2007.
White named a 35-strong squad which includes former England number eight Nathan Hughes as one of four uncapped players, while Josua Tuisova, Jiuta Wainiqolo and Caleb Muntz are also included.

No Jack Grealish, no problem - the rise of Everton's youngsters - BBC Sport
Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,
Players aged 24 or under are playing a higher proportion of minutes for Everton this season
ByMatthew Hobbs and Matt JonesBBC Sport journalists
AsEvertonprepared to faceNewcastlein the fourth round of the EFL Cup at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Thursday, the stakes were high.
A quarter-final tie against League Two opposition in Fleetwood awaited the winner, and a fanbase starved of trophies began to look ahead - albeit, for some, through covered eyes.
Then, in the build-up to the match, it was revealedJack Grealish had been dropped from the squadover what is understood to have been an unauthorised absence from training.
The unwanted headline threatened to derail preparations for the latest round of a competition that perhaps offersEverton's best chance of winning a trophy for the first time in 31 years.
Instead, the club's younger players came to the fore, led by the influential Hayden Hackney.
A £16.5m summer signing from Middlesbrough, the 24-year-old made light of his inexperience at the highest level against a strongNewcastleXI, assisting James Garner's opening goal before scoringEverton's second with a close-range volley.
Hackney, though, has needed to be patient early in hisEvertoncareer.
After starting the opening game of the season - a 2-0 win againstCrystal Palace- his only subsequent start prior to Thursday's cup victory was in the third round of the same competition against Wolves.
The central midfielder is not known for being prolific - the fourth-round win was only the second time in his career he had scored and assisted in the same game - but he knitted together phases of possession and carried the ball with the confidence that led to him being named Championship player of the year last season.
David Moyes, though, is a demanding manager and one perfectly prepared to keep young feet on the ground.
"I thought there were bits of his game that were very good," said theEvertonboss. "Getting a goal was great. There were other bits where I didn't think it was where it was [supposed to be].
"But I see this as a bit of bringing in Championship players, getting them used to the Premier League. A couple of times he got caught on the ball.
"But I really enjoyed bits. He gave us a bit of an attacking play, getting into the box, and obviously getting the goal was really good. A really good assist from Thierno Barry as well, to be fair."
While Hackney was ably assisted by strong performances from Garner and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall inEverton's midfield, the threadbare nature of the Toffees' squad means the development and contribution of the club's younger players could prove crucial in any success this season.
Of the 10 players signed on permanent deals since Moyes rejoined the club in January 2025, seven are aged 24 or under, including Barry.
The France Under-21 international is playing just a third season in a top-five European league after joining from Villarreal in July 2025, but his introduction to elite football has been more pressurised because ofEverton's lack of options up front.
Barry is the club's only specialist centre-forward, starting every match and playing 918 minutes this season. His tally of seven goals is already just one off his total from last season, despite playing 30 fewer matches.
Evertonhave recorded 24 big chances, and Barry has been involved in 15 of them (62.5%).
Whiles Moyes' hand has been somewhat forced in giving Barry game time because of a lack of alternatives, there has been a broader indication he is more prepared to back the younger members of his squad this season.
The average age ofEverton's starting XI in the Premier League has dropped by almost 18 months this season to 26 years and 216 days.
The departure of veteran midfielder Idrissa Gueye has made a difference but first-team players aged 24 or under are playing a much higher proportion of Premier League minutes than in the previous campaign.
Moyes used just 22 players in the Premier League last season. He has already used 22 in this one.
Even the youngest players in the squad appear to have gained more trust. In 2025-26, players aged 21 or under totalled 1,088 minutes for the Toffees, a figure that has already been exceeded this season (1,206).
At 19, Harrison Armstrong is the youngest regular inEverton's senior squad. In January, he had completed a six-month loan spell at Preston and Moyes considered sending him back to Deepdale for the remainder of last season before slowly integrating him into the first team.
This season, the teenager has started every Premier League match.
Winger Tyler Dibling, 20, initially struggled after a £35m move from Southampton in the summer of 2025 but was positive in gettingEvertonon to the front foot on againstNewcastleon Thursday night.
Tyrique George joined on a permanent deal fromChelseain the summer after spending the second half of last season on loan atEvertonduring which he made only one league start.
The 20-year-old has already made five this season, scoring his first goal for the club in the 2-2 draw withManchester Unitedin September.
George also started the EFL Cup fixture last week and won back possession for the opening goal.
Merlin Rohl broke into the team towards the end of last season and the 24-year-old midfielder, who also signed permanently in the summer following an initial loan spell, has since been trusted to fillEverton's problem position of right-back.
After missing four games because of injury, he was immediately brought back into the starting XI againstChelsea. He was then preferred to the more experienced Ainsley Maitland-Niles at right-back for matches againstArsenalandNewcastle.
When asked if Grealish would return to the squad for Monday's rematch at St James' Park, Moyes said he would not reveal any team news, though there is no doubt that experience still counts among the 63-year-old's most valuable commodities.
Defender James Tarkowksi, 33, has been a standout performer so far this season, while the form of fellow senior players such as Jordan Pickford, 32, and Dewsbury-Hall, 28 remain critical to thisEvertonside.
But whenEvertonmeetNewcastlefor the second time in less than a week on Monday, Grealish could again miss out.
In his absence, younger heads were good enough to win a cup tie. It would be further indication of their growing influence if they were to repeat that result in the Premier League.

The Premier League champions were so far below their best that it was hard to believe this was the same team thatstormed to the title last termand looked hungry toretain the crownin the opening weeks of this season.
A victory at Anfield would restore Arsenal’s belief, but in-form Liverpool will be no pushovers, especially on their home turf.
Heading into the match on a five-game winning streak, Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool are in a confident mood, and the Reds can move within three points of the Gunners if they win this weekend’s marquee match-up.
Here’s everything you need to know about Liverpool vs Arsenal:
How have Premier League holders Arsenal fared this season?
Arsenal are second in the Premier League standings on 21 points after eight games, sitting behind leaders Manchester City on goal difference. The Gunners have won seven league games and lost just once – a 3-0 defeat at Brighton last month.
In the Champions League, they are seventh in the league standings with two wins and a draw.
However, they were knocked out of the League Cup in the fourth round after losing 5-3 on penalties to fourth-tier Fleetwood.
Bruno Guimaraes missed a penalty in the shootout, as Arsenal were knocked out of the League Cup by Fleetwood [Carl Recine/Getty Images]
How have Liverpool played this season?
Liverpool are fourth in the league standings on 15 points, six points off the top of the table. The Reds have won four games, drawn three and lost once.
In the Champions League, they are third with three wins in three, and have qualified for the League Cup quarterfinals afterbeating Chelsea 6-5 on penaltiesmidweek.
